item.title: Parliament passes HIV Bill allowing needles and syringes program
item.description: Mansi Chand , Rashika Kumar · 01/10/2026 The HIV/AIDS Amendment Bill 2026 has been passed by Parliament this afternoon, allowing people who use drugs to access sterile needles and syringes as part of efforts to prevent the spread of HIV. The 2011 legislation has been amended because the provision of sterile needles and syringes could not legally begin under the existing framework.
item.content:encoded:
Mansi Chand , Rashika Kumar · 01/10/2026

The HIV/AIDS Amendment Bill 2026 has been passed by Parliament this afternoon, allowing people who use drugs to access sterile needles and syringes as part of efforts to prevent the spread of HIV. The 2011 legislation has been amended because the provision of sterile needles and syringes could not legally begin under the existing framework.

Minister for Health, Doctor Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu says this allows authorised harm reduction programs to operate under written directions issued by the Minister.

He says the programs may include the free distribution of sterile needles and syringes, condoms and lubricants, access to pre-exposure prophylaxis or PrEP and post-exposure prophylaxis or PEP drugs, counselling and HIV awareness materials.

The programs may also provide for the safe return and disposal of used needles and syringes and referrals to HIV treatment, rehabilitation, mental health and other health and social support services.

Lalabalavu says peer outreach workers will play a central role in distributing sterile needles and syringes and collecting used equipment for safe disposal.

He says the services are expected to be delivered through sexual and reproductive health and HIV clinics, other government clinics, non-governmental partners and interested private pharmacies.

The Minister stresses that the proposed changes do not legalise illicit drugs or authorise drug trafficking, supply, manufacture, cultivation, importation or exportation.

He says legal protections under the amendment will only apply to people carrying out activities reasonably necessary for an authorised harm reduction program.

While supporting the Bill, Assistant Minister for Health, Penioni Ravunawa says the amendment will provide legal protection for ministerially directed harm reduction programmes, including the provision of sterile needles and syringes to people who inject drugs to reduce the sharing of contaminated equipment.

He says the Ministry has prepared for the rollout, with commodities procured, service providers identified and operational standards prepared.

Ravunawa says this will also provide opportunities for HIV testing, connecting people to treatment and referring them for drug dependence support and rehabilitation.

Opposition MP Alvick Maharaj has supported the HIV/AIDS Amendment Bill 2026 but says there is a gap in the proposed legislation regarding legal protection for retail pharmacies that sell needles and syringes.

He says the legislation is an urgent step forward and allowing the free distribution of sterile needles and syringes will help reduce the risk of HIV transmission through the sharing of contaminated injecting equipment.

However, he says the proposed provisions cover the free distribution of needles and syringes under authorised harm reduction programmes but do not explicitly provide the same protection to retail pharmacies selling them.

He says this could become an issue when government-provided supplies are unavailable and people seek to purchase sterile needles and syringes from pharmacies.

Maharaj says the protection should be clarified or expanded to cover responsible retail sales where the equipment is being accessed for the same harm reduction purpose.

He says closing this gap would ensure pharmacies are protected whether they provide needles and syringes through a government-backed free initiative or responsible retail channels.

Minister for Women and Children Sashi Kiran says Fiji's response to HIV must address social vulnerabilities such as poverty, homelessness, substance dependence, mental health challenges, family violence and social exclusion.

Kiran says a key provision of the proposed legislation will allow harm reduction programmes to facilitate referrals to HIV treatment, rehabilitation, mental health services and wider health and social support systems.

She stresses that allowing sterile injecting equipment to be provided through regulated and approved harm reduction programmes is not about encouraging drug use but the objective is to prevent HIV transmission, illness and death while creating opportunities for treatment, rehabilitation and recovery.

She says provisions for the safe return and management of needles and syringes will also reduce the risk of accidental needle-stick injuries and protect health workers, municipal and waste management workers, Police and the wider public.

Kiran says enabling vulnerable people, including people who inject drugs, to connect with healthcare rather than remain hidden will help prevent infections and protect families.

Opposition MP Praveen Bala says if the initiative is about saving lives, they will support it and will not cause any delay.

Bala says people living with HIV should not be stigmatised, as stigma can drive people away from seeking support.

Assistant Minister for Transport Naisa Tuinaceva says the amendment does not legalise drugs but is aimed at preventing the further spread of HIV.

He says the measure is focused on protecting lives and reducing the risk of HIV transmission.

item.title: WATCH : fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan ft. Waisale Serevi
item.description: Fiji 7s rugby legend and icon Waisale Serevi appeared on fijivillage Straight Talk With Vijay Narayan. The show focused on Serevi's journey right from growing up in Nasole to becoming a rugby powerhouse in the world.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji 7s rugby legend and icon Waisale Serevi appeared on fijivillage Straight Talk With Vijay Narayan.

The show focused on Serevi's journey right from growing up in Nasole to becoming a rugby powerhouse in the world.

Serevi spoke on his many successes and challenges here and abroad, and the pressure on carrying the weight of the nation when taking part in rugby tournaments.

He also spoke on the serious issues affecting our people like drugs and HIV.

Serevi also shared his political ambitions and his plans for the future.

item.title: CJ Temo and CR Bainivalu remain silent after 2 cases of missing cocaine amounting to $50M
item.description: Chief Justice, Salesi Temo and Chief Registrar, Tomasi Bainivalu remain silent after the two cases of breaches at the Suva High Court Exhibit Room which has resulted in the disappearance of $50 million of cocaine from March to this month. fijivillage News has asked the Chief Justice and Chief Registrar what steps are being taken to ensure the person involved in taking the drugs from the exhibit ro
item.content:encoded:
Chief Justice, Salesi Temo and Chief Registrar, Tomasi Bainivalu remain silent after the two cases of breaches at the Suva High Court Exhibit Room which has resulted in the disappearance of $50 million of cocaine from March to this month.

fijivillage News has asked the Chief Justice and Chief Registrar what steps are being taken to ensure the person involved in taking the drugs from the exhibit room is apprehended.

We have also asked why the CCTV cameras were not operational and who was providing security at the exhibit room.

fijivillage News has also asked whether a full audit will be done for all the court exhibit rooms and whether all the drug exhibits will be tested.

All questions are being referred to Police.

The Police Forensics Team was at the court house today conducting investigations.

item.title: Yaqona farmers and stakeholders get another opportunity to make submissions on Kava Bill
item.description: Priya Nand , Mikaele Liga , Karishma Kumari · 01/10/2026 Yaqona farmers, traders, exporters and other stakeholders will have another opportunity to raise their concerns and recommendations on the proposed Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026 after its second reading in Parliament and referral to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights.
item.content:encoded:
Priya Nand , Mikaele Liga , Karishma Kumari · 01/10/2026

Yaqona farmers, traders, exporters and other stakeholders will have another opportunity to raise their concerns and recommendations on the proposed Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026 after its second reading in Parliament and referral to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights.

Government and Opposition MPs have supported the Bill’s objectives while raising issues around farmer protection, regulation and the future growth of the industry.

Minister for Agriculture Tomasi Tunabuna says more than 17,000 yaqona farmers in the country are expected to benefit from the proposed legislation.

Tunabuna says 93 percent of farmers in the country rely on yaqona for their income, while 1,015.7 tonnes were exported in 2025.

He says the Bill will protect the interests of farmers, regulate the sale of grog and provide greater public accountability.

He says the legislation will also help ensure the sustainability of the industry and provide more income and employment opportunities.

Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says the Bill has the potential to develop the sector into a billion-dollar industry.

Kamikamica says k ava exports in 2025 reached a total value of $79 million, while imports were valued at $48 million and local consumption reached $230 million.

He says the total value of the industry has reached about half a billion dollars, positioning kava as a major economic commodity.

He says the Bill will provide a clearly defined and structured process for farmers, exporters, importers and local users while safeguarding the safety and quality of kava.

Kamikamica says the Bill would also put more money into the pockets of farmers.

Minister for Foreign Affairs and External Trade, Sakiasi Ditoka says farmers will remain at the centre of the Bill.

He says farmers will become the brand of their own product and has expressed his full support for the legislation.

Assistant Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Sakiusa Tubuna says the Bill will ensure the proper management of yaqona as the industry works towards meeting regional and global standards.

Minister for Education Aseri Radrodro says yaqona is an important part of Fiji’s national life and is deeply connected to culture, traditions, community relationships and the livelihoods of thousands of Fijians.

However, he stresses that children and school students must be protected, with a clear distinction between the traditional and cultural use of yaqona by adults and its consumption by children and school students.

Radrodro says where the law prohibits the sale or supply of yaqona to children, this should be strongly supported and effectively enforced.

Opposition MP Jone Usamate says although he supports the Bill, Fiji has not been able to get the optimal benefits from yaqona despite its growing popularity around the world.

He says the legislation should ensure farmers receive a greater share of the financial benefits generated by the industry.

Usamate says Fiji should also build a strong identity and reputation around its yaqona so that it can attract premium prices internationally.

National Federation Party Leader Professor Biman Prasad also supports the Bill but is urging the Parliamentary Standing Committee to ensure regulations do not place unnecessary compliance costs and burdens on yaqona producers.

Professor Prasad says the Standing Committee should spend considerable time consulting yaqona producers, exporters and importers before the legislation is finalised.

He says regulations and compliance requirements need to protect the quality of Fiji’s yaqona, its brand and export potential without discouraging those involved in the industry.

Opposition MP Rinesh Sharma says farmers should benefit through better market access, improved quality, stronger protection of Fiji’s yaqona and better returns.

Sharma says t he proposed 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council, comprising government and private-sector representatives, will bring different perspectives into decision-making.

However, he says his main concern is ensuring the framework works for small farmers and does not place an unnecessary financial burden on them through fees and levies.

Opposition MP Premila Kumar says she supports a regulatory framework that improves quality, protects Fiji’s reputation, strengthens confidence in exports and allows farmers to benefit from growing markets.

However, Kumar raised concerns that several important matters, including registration requirements, fees and licensing conditions, are being left to regulations rather than being clearly set out in the Bill.

She says a s mall farmer selling a small quantity of yaqona should not face the same regulatory burden as a large commercial exporter.

item.title: Lal says Constitution Amendment Bill weakens key democratic safeguards
item.description: The Centre for Democracy and Dialogue says its preliminary analysis of the Fiji Government's Constitution Amendment Bill shows significant changes from the Constitution Review Commission’s draft, including the removal or weakening of several democratic and accountability safeguards. Centre for Democracy and Dialogue Chief Executive Officer Nilesh Lal says while the Constitution Amendment Bill reta
item.content:encoded:
The Centre for Democracy and Dialogue says its preliminary analysis of the Fiji Government's Constitution Amendment Bill shows significant changes from the Constitution Review Commission’s draft, including the removal or weakening of several democratic and accountability safeguards.

Centre for Democracy and Dialogue Chief Executive Officer Nilesh Lal says while the Constitution Amendment Bill retains some of the broad structure of the Constitution Review Commission's Draft Bill, it does not meaningfully address what the Centre for Democracy and Dialogue considers the excessive concentration of power in the Executive under the 2013 Constitution.

Lal says the Government's Constitution Amendment Bill removes the proposed limit on the Prime Minister’s tenure and the limit on the size of Cabinet as proposed by the Review Commission.

The CRC Amendment Bill proposed that Cabinet consist of the Prime Minister and up to 14 Ministers and that a person could not serve as Prime Minister more than twice.

However, under Section 110 of the Constitution Amendment Bill , the Prime Minister would determine the number of Ministers.

Lal says another significant change concerns the Constitutional Offices Commission.

He says the CRC Amendment Bill proposed a five-member COC appointed through an independent appointments committee, while the Government draft makes the serving Prime Minister the chair of the commission alongside the Attorney-General.

Lal says the Government would also have influence over the appointment of two further members, which he says would give it a four-to-two majority over the Opposition.

They say the COC is responsible for appointments to several key constitutional offices, including the Electoral Commission, Supervisor of Elections, Public Service Commission, Police Commissioner, Corrections Commissioner, RFMF Commander, Auditor-General, Reserve Bank Governor and Ombudsman.

The Centre also says provisions proposed by the CRC on political parties, political finance and campaigning have been removed from the Government draft.

The CRC Amendment Bill included constitutional provisions covering political party conduct, donations, disclosure requirements and access to State-owned media.

Lal says leaving these matters to ordinary law could allow future parliamentary majorities to change the rules.

The Centre says the Bill of Rights in the Constitution Amendment Bill generally provides stronger protections than the current Constitution but has raised concern over Section 40, which expressly permits lawful and moderate chastisement of children for correction.

Lal describes this as a regression from both the CRC draft and the 2013 Constitution.

Centre says other reforms proposed by the CRC that have been removed include stronger measures for women’s representation, a National Planning Commission, a National Infrastructure Council, a constitutionally mandated Opposition chair of the Public Accounts Committee, an independent Constitution Implementation Commission and a pluralistic Presidential Appointment Commission.

Lal says these changes raise questions about how the Constitution Amendment Bill was prepared and why it differs significantly from the CRC Amendment Bill submitted on 31st August.

He is questioning who wrote the Government's Constitution Amendment Bill, what was the basis for the changes from the CRC Amendment Bill and how the substantially different constitutional text was produced within a short period.

The Centre says its assessment is preliminary and argues that the changes substantially dilute safeguards proposed by the CRC against the concentration and abuse of State power.
